questions.stem: A successful collision requires the particles to collide with

options.text: Sufficient energy and the correct orientation
options.explanation: Both conditions together let bonds break and new bonds form.

options.text: High speed only, whatever the direction
options.explanation: Energy without orientation leaves the collision ineffective.

options.text: Correct orientation only, whatever the energy
options.explanation: Orientation without the activation energy still bounces the pair apart.

options.text: Identical masses in each collision
options.explanation: Particle masses need not match for reaction.

questions.stem: An unsuccessful collision is one in which the particles

options.text: Stick together as an intermediate
options.explanation: Unsuccessful collisions separate the particles again.

options.text: Bounce apart because of wrong orientation or too little energy
options.explanation: Both failure routes leave the reactants unchanged.

options.text: Always combine to form a temporary compound
options.explanation: No product forms in an unsuccessful collision.

options.text: Transfer all their energy to the surroundings
options.explanation: Energy transfer is not the definition of failure here.

questions.stem: The rate of a chemical reaction is ultimately determined by

options.text: The mass of the largest reactant particle
options.explanation: Mass is not the direct determinant.

options.text: The temperature alone in every case
options.explanation: Temperature matters, but only through the collision factors it feeds.

options.text: The number of successful collisions per unit time
options.explanation: Rate counts effective collisions, not raw collision numbers.

options.text: The total number of collisions however weak
options.explanation: Most collisions fail; counting them overstates the rate.

questions.stem: Which list gives the three rate-controlling factors named in collision theory?

options.text: Pressure, catalysts and light intensity
options.explanation: These are condition levers, not the theory's named trio.

options.text: Molar mass, density and polarity
options.explanation: None of these is the collision-theory trio.

options.text: Surface area, temperature and a colour change
options.explanation: The colour change is a measuring method, not a factor.

options.text: Collision frequency, collision energy, activation energy
options.explanation: These three together decide how many collisions succeed.

questions.stem: Bonds in the reactants break and new bonds form only when

options.text: A collision carries at least the activation energy and correct geometry
options.explanation: The energy hurdle and orientation together allow bond reorganisation.

options.text: Any collision occurs, however gentle
options.explanation: Gentle collisions bounce off without reaction.

options.text: The particles are at absolute rest
options.explanation: Resting particles do not collide at all.

options.text: A catalyst is always present
options.explanation: Catalysts help but uncatalysed successful collisions still occur.

questions.stem: State the two conditions for an effective collision.
questions.modelAnswer: The particles must collide with energy at least equal to the activation energy and in the correct orientation.

questions.stem: Define an unsuccessful collision.
questions.modelAnswer: A collision in which the particles lack the energy or the orientation needed to react, so they bounce apart without forming products.

questions.stem: Explain why most collisions do not lead to reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Most colliding pairs either lack the minimum activation energy or meet in an unproductive orientation, so bonds stay intact and the particles separate unchanged.

questions.stem: A reaction between two gases suddenly speeds up when the mixture is compressed. Explain using collision theory.
questions.modelAnswer: Compression packs the same particles into a smaller volume, raising collision frequency; with the same fraction of successful collisions, more effective collisions occur per unit time and the rate rises.

questions.stem: Increasing the concentration of a solution increases rate because

options.text: The particles change orientation more efficiently
options.explanation: Orientation is unaffected by concentration.

options.text: More particles occupy the same volume, so collisions happen more often
options.explanation: Crowding raises collision frequency, hence more successful collisions per unit time.

options.text: Each collision carries more energy
options.explanation: Concentration does not change the energy of individual collisions.

options.text: The activation energy becomes smaller
options.explanation: Ea is fixed for a given reaction at a given temperature.

questions.stem: Raising the pressure of a gas reaction raises rate because

options.text: The activation energy barrier drops
options.explanation: The barrier is a property of the reaction, not the pressure.

options.text: Fewer particles are needed for the reaction
options.explanation: Stoichiometry is unchanged by pressure.

options.text: The same number of particles now sits in a smaller volume, colliding more often
options.explanation: Compression concentrates the particles, lifting collision frequency.

options.text: The molecules gain kinetic energy from compression
options.explanation: Kinetic energy rises with temperature, not with pressure at fixed T.

questions.stem: Which condition raises BOTH collision frequency and collision energy?

options.text: Increasing the concentration
options.explanation: Concentration raises frequency only.

options.text: Grinding a solid into powder
options.explanation: Surface area raises frequency only.

options.text: Adding an inert gas at constant volume
options.explanation: Inert gas barely changes the reactant collision count.

options.text: Increasing the temperature
options.explanation: Heat raises kinetic energy, speeding particles so they meet more often and hit harder.

questions.stem: Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant works by

options.text: Exposing more particles for collision at the interface
options.explanation: More available surface means more collision opportunities per unit time.

options.text: Lowering the activation energy of the reaction
options.explanation: Ea is unchanged by subdivision.

options.text: Increasing the energy of each collision
options.explanation: Collision energy is set by temperature, not surface area.

options.text: Dissolving the solid faster
options.explanation: Dissolution is not the mechanism for a solid-solid or solid-gas reaction.

questions.stem: A mixture has frequent collisions yet reacts slowly. The best explanation is

options.text: The activation energy is zero
options.explanation: With zero Ea almost every energetic collision would succeed.

options.text: Most collisions lack sufficient energy to overcome the activation energy
options.explanation: High frequency with low success still gives a slow rate.

options.text: The collisions are too frequent to succeed
options.explanation: There is no such effect; frequency helps.

options.text: The particles are colliding in the wrong container
options.explanation: Container choice is not a collision-theory factor.

questions.stem: State four ways to increase collision frequency.
questions.modelAnswer: Increase concentration, increase pressure, increase temperature, or increase the surface area of the reacting particles.

questions.stem: Define collision frequency.
questions.modelAnswer: The number of collisions between reactant particles per unit time in the system.

questions.stem: Explain why temperature is the most powerful of the four frequency levers.
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature raises collision frequency and also increases the proportion of collisions carrying at least the activation energy, so it lifts both factors that decide the rate.

questions.stem: Marble chips react faster as powder than as lumps with the same acid. Explain with collision theory, and state one lever the student must keep constant for a fair test.
questions.modelAnswer: Powder exposes far more surface, so more acid particles collide with exposed solid per unit time, raising successful collisions; concentration and temperature must be kept constant for the comparison to be fair.

questions.stem: Activation energy is

options.text: The energy of the products minus the reactants
options.explanation: That describes ΔH, not the barrier height.

options.text: The average kinetic energy of the mixture
options.explanation: The average sits below Ea for most reactions; Ea is the threshold.

options.text: The minimum energy colliding particles must possess for a reaction to occur
options.explanation: Below Ea, no collision can convert reactants into products.

options.text: The total energy released by an exothermic reaction
options.explanation: That is the enthalpy change, not Ea.

questions.stem: On an energy profile for an endothermic reaction, the reactants sit

options.text: Higher than the products, giving a small barrier
options.explanation: That describes the exothermic profile.

options.text: At the same level as the products
options.explanation: Endothermic reactions have a net energy rise.

options.text: At the curve's maximum
options.explanation: The maximum is the transition state, not the reactants.

options.text: Lower than the products, giving a relatively larger activation energy
options.explanation: Climbing uphill needs a bigger barrier, matching endothermic absorption.

questions.stem: A collision with perfect orientation still fails when

options.text: Its energy is below the activation energy
options.explanation: Both conditions are required; failing one is enough to bounce the pair apart.

options.text: The particles are gases
options.explanation: Gas-phase collisions succeed regularly when conditions are met.

options.text: The temperature is high
options.explanation: High temperature raises success, not failure.

options.text: A catalyst is absent
options.explanation: Catalysis is optional; uncatalysed successful collisions occur.

questions.stem: Why is the exothermic barrier comparatively small?

options.text: Products in exothermic reactions have no energy
options.explanation: Products still carry energy; they are simply lower than reactants.

options.text: The reactants already sit higher in energy than the products
options.explanation: Starting high means less climb to the transition state.

options.text: Exothermic reactions release no energy
options.explanation: They release the surplus after the barrier is crossed.

options.text: Their particles always collide harder
options.explanation: Collision energy depends on temperature, not reaction type.

questions.stem: Rate experiments commonly measure reaction progress by tracking

options.text: The activation energy directly
options.explanation: Ea is deduced from analysis, not read during the run.

options.text: The particle orientation with a camera
options.explanation: Orientation is a model concept, not a lab measurement.

options.text: Reactant lost, product formed, a colour change, or precipitate formation timing
options.explanation: All four translate successful collisions into observable change.

options.text: Only the mass of the catalyst
options.explanation: Catalyst mass is constant and uninformative here.

questions.stem: Define activation energy.
questions.modelAnswer: The minimum energy that reactant particles must possess for a collision to lead to reaction.

questions.stem: Compare the activation energy of exothermic and endothermic reactions.
questions.modelAnswer: Exothermic reactions have a relatively small Ea because reactants start above products; endothermic reactions have a relatively larger Ea because reactants start below products.

questions.stem: Explain why a catalyst lowers Ea without changing collision frequency.
questions.modelAnswer: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower energy barrier, so the same collision population now has a larger fraction above the reduced Ea - frequency is untouched, success fraction rises.

questions.stem: Two reactions share identical conditions and collision frequencies, but reaction A is much faster. Sketch reasoning in words comparing their Ea values.
questions.modelAnswer: Reaction A must have the lower activation energy: with equal collision counts, the mixture whose energy distribution clears the smaller barrier yields far more successful collisions per unit time.
